title: Government caps Malaysia migration cost at Tk 1.54 lakh
excerpt: Workers have paid up to Tk 8 lakh before. State agency BOESL has begun picking 112 workers for zero-cost jobs.

image.alt: Passengers walking across the apron at Jashore airport, seen from behind

content:
The government has capped the cost for workers going to Malaysia at Tk 1.54 lakh (about US$1,250), Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said at Probashi Kalyan Bhaban in Dhaka on Thursday, 12 November, The Daily Star reported. Workers have previously paid Tk 7 lakh to Tk 8 lakh.

What was announced

  • Cap: Tk 1.54 lakh for workers recruited through private agencies. Agencies had suggested Tk 2 lakh to Tk 2.5 lakh, which the minister said the government has not accepted.
  • Penalties: agencies that overcharge face legal action, including action on their licences.
  • Checks on jobs: agencies must give each worker's employer, job, contract length and recruitment arrangements so the government can confirm the job is real.
  • Zero-cost route: the state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) has begun selecting 112 workers whose costs Malaysian employers will pay. This is the first phase of a plan to send 10,000 workers through BOESL.
  • Medical tests: the fee is fixed at Tk 8,000. Bangladesh objected to some of the 51 proposed medical centres, and a final list was expected within days.

A nine-member Malaysian team began tests and interviews on 12 November and continues until 15 November. Officials said the first group could leave before December. They also warned that anyone, including BOESL staff, caught taking money from candidates would face legal action, after reports that middlemen were asking for Tk 5 lakh to Tk 6 lakh.

Malaysia stopped hiring Bangladeshi workers on 31 May 2024 over high costs and irregularities. It reopened recruitment earlier this month.

Why it matters

Debt from recruitment fees is a main driver of exploitation and forced labour among migrant workers. Migrant rights NGOs and legal aid groups will be key to telling jobseekers the official cap and the zero-cost BOESL route, and to helping workers report agencies or middlemen who charge more.

What to watch

The final list of approved medical centres, the departure of the first BOESL group, and whether the ministry acts against agencies that charge above the cap.

Sources
